title: Libraries, Museums & Archives
tagline: Librarians, archivists, and curators — the keepers and connectors of knowledge and culture.
summary: The GLAM sector (galleries, libraries, archives, museums) preserves and shares knowledge: librarians connect people to information, archivists preserve records, curators interpret collections. This roadmap covers the MLIS path, the archives and museum tracks, and the craft of public service in cultural institutions.

sources.label: O*NET — Librarians and Media Collections Specialists (25-1012.00)

detail.description: Galleries, libraries, archives, and museums (GLAM) share a mission — collecting, preserving, and connecting people to knowledge and culture — with distinct roles and credentials per institution type.
detail.why: These are public-service careers for the curious: quieter than most, deeply mission-driven, and surprisingly varied between public, academic, and museum settings.
learn: Read the BLS OOH librarian profile
Compare public, academic, school, and special libraries
Visit one library, one archive, and one museum this month
Note which function pulls you: people, collections, or systems

resources.title: O*NET — Librarians and Media Collections Specialists

detail.description: Public libraries serve everyone; academic libraries serve campuses; school libraries serve students; special libraries (law, medical, corporate) serve organizations; museums and archives hold collections.
detail.why: Your institution type shapes pace, patrons, credentials, and job availability — pick with your temperament.
learn: List the institution types in your region and visit two
Compare patron interactions per type
Note degree expectations per type
Pick a primary and backup target

detail.description: The role families: library assistants/technicians (entry), librarians (MLIS-credentialed), archivists, curators, museum technicians, and conservators — plus programming and administration layers.
detail.why: Knowing which role matches your education stage tells you exactly what to do next — assistant now, MLIS later is a classic path.
learn: Map roles vs required degrees
Check local job postings for each role
Note O*NET tasks for librarian and archivist roles
Choose your entry point

detail.description: The sector's core values: intellectual freedom, equitable access, privacy of patrons, and service to the whole community — not just the visitors who look like staff.
detail.why: These values define the profession's identity and show up in daily decisions, hiring interviews, and community trust.
learn: Read the American Library Association's Code of Ethics
Observe how libraries serve unhoused patrons
Reflect on privacy vs safety tensions
Note inclusive-service examples you admire

detail.description: Assistants and technicians run daily operations: circulation, shelving, patron accounts, basic reference, and program support — the field's practical entry without a master's.
detail.why: It pays to learn the floor first: assistant experience strengthens MLIS applications and confirms fit.
learn: Apply for assistant/technician openings locally
Learn the ILS (library system) basics fast
Practice warm reference conversations
Volunteer for programs and events

resources.title: BLS OOH — Library Technicians and Assistants

detail.description: Librarian roles require the Master of Library and Information Science (ALA-accredited), usually 1.5–3 years, often online, covering reference, cataloging, management, and technology.
detail.why: The MLIS is the profession's license-equivalent — choosing an accredited, affordable program with the right specialization matters enormously.
learn: Verify ALA accreditation for any program
Compare specializations: youth, archives, data, UX
Check part-time/online feasibility while working
Research scholarships and assistantships

detail.description: Librarians specialize: reference and adult services, children's and teen services, technical services (cataloging/acquisitions), digital services, and outreach — each a different daily rhythm.
detail.why: Specialization is how librarians find their niche — from toddler story time to legal research support.
learn: Sample one specialization's daily tasks via informational interviews
Practice reference interviews (the patron's real question)
Build one program proposal end-to-end
Learn your community's demographics and needs
tasks: Administer libraries and perform related library services; work in a variety of settings including public libraries, schools, and government agencies.

detail.description: The systems craft: cataloging standards (MARC-style records), classification, subject headings, and modern metadata for digital collections — making things findable.
detail.why: Technical-services and digital-collection careers are built on metadata fluency — the field's systems track.
learn: Understand what a catalog record contains and why
Practice basic metadata description for a photo collection
Learn controlled vocabularies conceptually
Explore digital-collection platforms in demo mode

detail.description: Archivists appraise, arrange, describe, and preserve permanent records — institutional histories, manuscripts, photographs — guided by archival standards and finding aids.
detail.why: Archives suit meticulous, history-loving organizers; employers span universities, governments, corporations, and historical societies.
learn: Read about archival appraisal and arrangement basics
Volunteer to process a small collection
Learn what a finding aid looks like
Note the archives credential expectations (MLIS/history MA)

detail.description: Curators and museum technicians acquire, research, care for, and interpret collections — registrars track objects, conservators preserve them, educators bring them to the public.
detail.why: Museums need both scholarly depth and hands-on care — the field rewards people who start volunteering in collections departments.
learn: Volunteer at a local museum in collections or education
Learn object-handling and condition-reporting basics
Note the graduate degree norms for curatorial tracks
Write one mock exhibit label

resources.title: BLS OOH — Archivists, Curators, and Museum Workers

detail.description: Libraries live through their programs: story times, classes, book clubs, job-help, and community partnerships — planned, promoted, and measured like small events.
detail.why: Programming is how libraries prove their value to funders — strong programmers get promoted.
learn: Design a 4-week program series with goals
Practice running one program end-to-end
Promote via partners, not just flyers
Measure attendance and outcomes honestly

detail.description: The reference craft: the reference interview, search strategy, database fluency, source evaluation, and teaching patrons to fish rather than just handing answers.
detail.why: Research skill is the librarian's core product — and it transfers to any knowledge role.
learn: Practice the reference interview on friends' real questions
Master 3 research databases deeply
Build search strategies: keywords, filters, citation chasing
Evaluate sources with a repeatable rubric

detail.description: Digitization and digital preservation: scanning standards, rights clearance, metadata, and long-term digital preservation — the sector's growth frontier.
detail.why: Institutions are racing to digitize and preserve digital-born material — digital-curation skills are the most future-proof in the sector.
learn: Volunteer on a digitization project
Learn scanning standards and quality checks
Understand rights clearance basics
Explore preservation formats and metadata schemas

detail.description: Directors and department heads manage budgets, staff, boards, buildings, and community politics — leadership that protects the institution's mission.
detail.why: Administrators decide what's possible; the sector needs leaders who came up through service.
learn: Learn public-library funding basics (millages, budgets)
Practice board-meeting communication
Manage one small budget or grant
Shadow a library or museum director

detail.description: Cultural institutions survive on grants, friends-groups, and donors: writing applications, reporting outcomes, and building funder relationships.
detail.why: Grant-writing ability makes you indispensable — institutions compete hard for people who bring money in.
learn: Write one mock grant application to a real funder
Learn outcome reporting basics
Join the friends-group or development committee
Study one successful institutional grant

detail.description: Libraries and museums face funding fights and censorship challenges — advocacy means demonstrating value to boards, voters, and legislatures with stories and data.
detail.why: The sector's future is decided in budget hearings; staff who can advocate protect their own institutions.
learn: Learn your library's funding structure
Collect impact stories with consent
Practice a 3-minute value pitch
Attend one budget or board meeting

detail.description: Conservators combine art history and chemistry to preserve objects — a specialized graduate-trained path within museums for the scientifically minded.
detail.why: Conservation is the sector's rarest, most scientific craft — a real option for lab-loving art people.
learn: Research conservation graduate program prerequisites (chemistry required)
Volunteer in a objects lab if accessible
Learn preventive-care basics: light, humidity, pests
Note the portfolio expectations

detail.description: Ladders: assistant → librarian/curator → senior/department head → director; archives: processing archivist → collections manager → head of special collections.
detail.why: The sector moves slowly but stably — deliberate credentialing and public-service visibility drive advancement.
learn: Map the ladder in your target institution type
Identify the degree/certificate your next rung needs
Join the professional association early (student rates)
Present at a conference or write a post

detail.description: Honest market: librarian positions are competitive and often part-time first; archives and museums pay modestly; flexibility on location and institution type multiplies options.
detail.why: Going in clear-eyed — with a specialization the market wants (digital, youth, health) — is what turns the degree into a job.
learn: Count real postings for your specialization over a month
Stay geographically flexible early in your career
Build a portfolio of programs/projects, not just a resume
Consider adjacent employers (schools, corporate archives)

detail.description: Modern GLAM work is technical: ILS platforms, digital preservation systems, discovery layers, and helping patrons with everything from printers to privacy online.
detail.why: The stereotype-breaking truth: technology comfort is among the most requested skills in every posting.
learn: Learn one ILS in demo mode
Practice patient tech-help conversations
Follow digital-preservation news monthly
Offer a tech-help program at your library

detail.description: Exhibits, author talks, and community events bring collections alive: concept, curation, loans, promotion, and accessibility — museum-adjacent craft inside libraries too.
detail.why: Event and exhibit experience demonstrates curation plus project management — a promotion-worthy combination.
learn: Curate a small display from your collection
Run one author talk or community event
Learn accessibility standards for exhibits
Document attendance and feedback
